name: Design a Hotel Reservation System
intent: Sell room-nights without ever promising the same room twice, let people search any date range quickly, and keep a room held while a guest pays.
codeTitle: per-night inventory with holds and idempotent booking
finalIntro: One guest booking three nights while others compete for the last rooms.
prompt: Design the booking system for a chain with 20,000 hotels. Guests search by city and dates, pick a room type, pay, and get a confirmation. A stay covers several nights, rooms of a type are interchangeable, and the last rooms of a popular weekend are fought over by many guests at once. A guest must never arrive to find the booking was not honoured because of a bug.
functional: Search hotels with a free room of a given type for a date range
Hold a room while the guest pays, then confirm the booking
Cancel a booking and give the rooms back
Let hotel staff change room counts, prices and block rooms for maintenance
Optionally sell a few more rooms than exist, according to a policy
nonFunctional: Never confirm more bookings than the hotel's limit for any night, even with many simultaneous requests
A search answers in under 300 ms, and it may be a few seconds out of date
A booking is exact: the final check is always against the real inventory
A retry of the same booking request must not book twice or charge twice
Unpaid holds free their rooms automatically within minutes
Handle about 50 bookings per second at the peak and about 100 times as many searches

firstAttempt.text: One bookings table with a room number, a check-in date and a check-out date. To book, the app searches for a room of the type that has no overlapping booking, and then inserts a row for it. Availability is the same overlap query run for every hotel in the city.
limits: Two requests can both find the same room free and both insert, because the check and the insert are separate steps
The overlap query scans many rows for every search, and every search for a weekend hits the same table
There is no way to hold a room while the guest types a card number
A retried request after a timeout inserts a second booking
Selling a few rooms more than exist, on purpose, has nowhere to be expressed
One database serves searching, booking and hotel staff, so a busy search hurts bookings

steps.title: Store one inventory row per room type and night
steps.problem: Asking whether any room is free across a date range means comparing intervals against every booking, and interchangeable rooms make the individual room number irrelevant to the guest.
steps.fix: Sell a room type, not a room number. For each hotel, room type and night keep one row holding the capacity, the number sold, and the number on hold. A stay from the 16th to the 18th touches two rows, the nights of the 16th and the 17th, and the checkout day is not a night. Availability for a range is the smallest 'capacity minus sold minus held' over its nights. A room number is assigned at check-in, when the hotel knows who is leaving.
steps.tradeoff: Searching and booking become small lookups of a few rows, and double-booking turns into a counter that must not exceed a limit. A stay is now a set of rows, so the write for a long stay touches many rows, and the real room assignment is postponed to the front desk.

steps.title: Reserve all the nights with one conditional update
steps.problem: Reading the free count and then writing it back lets two guests both see one room left on a night, and both take it.
steps.fix: Do the check inside the write. For each night run 'UPDATE inventory SET held = held + 1 WHERE hotel = ? AND type = ? AND night = ? AND sold + held < limit', and look at the number of rows changed. All the nights are updated in one transaction, in a fixed order such as by date, so that two stays cannot wait on each other in a circle. If any night changes zero rows, the transaction rolls back and the guest is told that the room just went. A row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE does the same job, and an optimistic version column (the update succeeds only if the version has not changed) does it with a retry.
steps.tradeoff: The database serialises competing guests on each row, so the count can never pass its limit, whatever the number of app servers. A very popular night becomes a hot row and its throughput is bounded by how fast one row can be updated, so a rejection must be cheap and quick.

steps.title: Hold the rooms while the guest pays, and make requests idempotent
steps.problem: Payment takes a minute and can fail or be abandoned, and a mobile client that times out will send the request again.
steps.fix: Booking has two phases. First the service places a hold: the 'held' counters go up and a hold record stores the stay, the guest and an expiry time about ten minutes away. Then the guest pays, and on success the hold becomes a booking, moving the counters from 'held' to 'sold'. A sweeper releases holds whose time has passed. Every request carries an idempotency key (a unique id that makes a repeat harmless), and the hold record is created with that key as a unique value, so a repeat returns the earlier result instead of holding again. The payment call uses the same key.
steps.tradeoff: Rooms are not locked forever by people who walk away, and retries are safe. Held rooms are unavailable to others for the hold period, so a short hold sells more but annoys slow payers, and a payment that succeeds just after the hold expired needs a defined outcome, such as re-checking the inventory or refunding.

steps.title: Answer searches from a cache, and check again when booking
steps.problem: Guests look at about a hundred hotels for each one they book, and answering that from the inventory table would be most of the load.
steps.fix: Searches read an availability cache keyed by hotel, room type and date range, or a compact copy of the inventory kept per city, refreshed when inventory changes and expiring after a few seconds. The search page says 'only 2 left' from this copy. The booking path never trusts the cache. It runs the conditional update on the real rows, and if that fails the guest sees that the room has gone and is offered alternatives.
steps.tradeoff: Most traffic never touches the database, and search latency is low. The cache can be seconds old, so a guest sometimes clicks on a room that just sold, which is acceptable only because the final check is exact. A cache that says 'sold out' wrongly costs a sale, so staleness is allowed to err towards showing a room.

steps.title: Sell a few more rooms than exist, within a policy
steps.problem: Some guests cancel or do not arrive, so a hotel that sells exactly its rooms ends the night with empty ones that nobody can buy any more.
steps.fix: Make the limit a number the hotel controls instead of the capacity. The limit for a night is the capacity plus an overbooking allowance, set per hotel, type and night from the history of cancellations and no-shows, for example 3 percent for a business hotel on a weekday and nothing for a small inn on a festival weekend. The conditional update compares against this limit. The policy also says what happens when too many arrive: upgrade the guest to a better room, or move them to a partner hotel at the chain's cost.
steps.tradeoff: Rooms stop being wasted, and revenue rises. If the allowance is higher than the real cancellation rate, real guests are turned away at the desk, which costs money and trust, so the allowance is tuned from data, kept small, and cut on nights with a low cancellation rate.

steps.title: Publish booking events and keep partners in step
steps.problem: Travel sites, the hotel's own system and our cache all sell or show the same rooms, and each must hear about a booking, or a room gets sold twice in two places.
steps.fix: The booking transaction writes an event to an outbox in the same database commit, and a relay publishes it to a queue. Consumers update the availability cache, tell the channel manager (the tool that keeps partner sites in step) to close or reduce the room on partner sites, send the confirmation email and update revenue reports. Events carry a version and an id, so each consumer can ignore a repeat. Inbound bookings from partners go through the same conditional update, so a partner can never bypass the limit.
steps.tradeoff: Every channel learns about a booking within seconds without the booking transaction waiting for them, and nothing is lost on a crash. Partner sites are always a little behind, so the hotel keeps a small safety margin on channels, and a booking that arrives after a stale partner price needs a rule for who pays.

failures.scenario: Two guests book the last room for overlapping dates at the same moment
failures.impact: With a read followed by a write both succeed, and the hotel has two guests for one room on the night they share.
failures.answer: The conditional update on each night's row lets only one of them past the limit. The loser's transaction rolls back, including any nights it had already taken, and is offered other dates. Locking rows in date order keeps two stays from deadlocking.

failures.scenario: The client times out and sends the booking request again
failures.impact: Without protection the guest has two holds, and may pay twice.
failures.answer: The idempotency key is unique in the hold table, so the second request finds the first and returns its outcome. The payment provider receives the same key, so one charge is made even if the call is repeated.

failures.scenario: The guest pays after the hold has expired
failures.impact: The rooms may have gone to someone else, and the guest has been charged for nothing.
failures.answer: Confirmation checks that the hold is still live. If it is not, the service tries to take the rooms again with a new conditional update, and if that fails it asks the payment provider for a refund. A saga records each step so that a crash between payment and confirmation is repaired by a job.

failures.scenario: The availability cache is stale during a big event
failures.impact: Thousands of guests see a room that has just sold out and pile onto the same few rows.
failures.answer: The cache is allowed to be wrong because the booking path is exact, but the pile-on is limited by rate limits per hotel and by dropping the cache entry for a sold-out room as soon as the event arrives. A sold-out flag in the cache is set first, so most guests stop at the search page.

failures.scenario: Overbooking meets a night when everyone shows up
failures.impact: More guests arrive than rooms exist, and some are turned away (called walking a guest).
failures.answer: The policy was a bet on a cancellation rate, so it has a prepared answer: upgrade a guest, or book a nearby partner hotel and pay for it. The allowance for that hotel and night is lowered automatically when the walk-out rate goes over its target, and an alert tells revenue managers.

alternatives.title: How to stop double-booking

options.name: Conditional update on the inventory row
options.pro: One statement, no explicit lock held while the app thinks, and simple to reason about
options.con: A hot row is a bottleneck, and all nights of a stay must be updated together

options.name: Row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE
options.pro: Reads the values first, so the app can apply rules before the write
options.con: Holds a lock for the whole transaction, so slow code in it blocks everyone

options.name: Optimistic version number with retry
options.pro: No locks, and good when conflicts are rare
options.con: Under heavy competition for the last rooms most attempts fail and retry

options.name: A distributed lock per hotel and night
options.con: A second system that can fail or expire while the update is still running

alternatives.pick: A conditional update inside one transaction, with locks taken in date order. Reserve the other options for special cases.

alternatives.title: What to store

options.name: Bookings with dates, find overlaps
options.pro: Natural to model, and every booking is a record
options.con: Overlap queries are slow, and the rule 'at most N at once' is hard to enforce

options.name: Counters per room type and night
options.pro: Availability is a lookup, and the limit is one comparison
options.con: A lot of rows for a long horizon, and room numbers come later

options.name: Per-room per-night rows
options.pro: Each room is assigned immediately, so guests can ask for a specific room
options.con: Many more rows, and interchangeable rooms make guests compete over a single one

alternatives.pick: Counters per room type and night, plus a bookings table. Per-room rows only for a hotel that sells specific rooms.

alternatives.title: Where overbooking is applied

options.name: A fixed allowance as a percentage
options.pro: Easy to explain and to code
options.con: Ignores that cancellation rates differ by hotel, season and price

options.name: An allowance learned from history
options.pro: Close to the true rate, so few walk-outs and few empty rooms
options.con: Needs data, a model, and guard rails when it is wrong

alternatives.pick: A limit per hotel, type and night, set from history, with a hard cap and automatic cut when walk-outs rise.

alternatives.title: How long to hold the rooms

options.name: No hold: book on click and refund later
options.con: Payment failures and abandoned carts become refunds

options.name: A short hold of five to ten minutes
A long hold of an hour or more
options.pro: Friendly to guests who need approval

alternatives.pick: About ten minutes, extendable once during payment, with a sweeper to free expired holds.

quiz.question: The last double room is free on the night of 16 June. Two guests press 'book' at the same moment on different app servers, and the code reads the number free, checks it is above zero, and writes the new number. Both get a confirmation. What change stops this?
options: Wrap the read-and-write code in an in-memory lock inside each app server, so only one booking at a time can run
Read the number from a cache with a 1-second time to live, so that the second guest is likely to see the new figure at once
Run one update per night with a WHERE condition that sold + held is below the limit, and check rows changed
Read the count again after writing and cancel the newest booking if it has gone below zero
quiz.explanation: The check has to be part of the write, so the database lets only one request past the limit, whatever the number of servers. A lock in server memory does nothing between servers, a 1-second cache still leaves a window, and a check after the write leaves guests with confirmations that must then be taken back.

quiz.question: A 200-room business hotel sees about 6% cancellations and no-shows on weekdays, with a spread between 3% and 9%. For a festival weekend the rate is close to 1%. The revenue team wants to sell more than the capacity. Which policy fits?
options: The same 6% allowance for every night, because the yearly average is the best single predictor of the cancellation rate
A limit per hotel and night set from history, such as 4% on weekdays and none on the festival, cut if walk-outs rise
A 9% allowance for every night, so that even the worst weekday of cancellations does not leave a single room empty
No allowance at all, because turning a guest away at the desk costs more in trust than the empty rooms ever cost
quiz.explanation: The cancellation rate differs by night, and a safe allowance sits below the typical rate. A flat 6% or 9% would oversell the festival weekend by many rooms. No overbooking is safe but wastes the rooms of the likely cancellations, which is why a tuned and capped allowance is used.

quiz.question: A hold lasts 10 minutes. A guest's card payment goes through at minute 12, after the hold expired and the sweeper released the rooms. Another guest may or may not have taken them. What should the confirmation step do?
options: Confirm the booking anyway, because the guest has paid and the hotel can use its overbooking allowance to cover it
Refund the payment without checking the inventory, because an expired hold always means the rooms are gone
Raise the hold time to 60 minutes for all bookings, so that a payment cannot arrive after the hold has expired
Try to take the rooms again with a new conditional update, and only if that fails refund the payment and record each step
quiz.explanation: A late payment may find the rooms still free, so the service re-checks with the same exact update, and refunds only if it fails. Confirming blindly breaks the limit, an automatic refund loses sales that were still possible, and a 60-minute hold locks up stock on busy nights.
